Arkansas enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 26-8 overall and 13-5 in SEC play, with the official team cumulative report dated March 15, 2026 listing a 26-8 record, a 17-1 home mark, 5-5 away, and 4-2 on neutral floors. The same official Arkansas season page lists the SEC record at 13-5. As a profile snapshot, the Razorbacks average 89.9 points per game, shoot .500 from the field, .389 from three, and post a 1.9 assist-turnover ratio with only 9.0 turnovers per game; defensively they hold opponents to .453 overall and .317 from three while producing 7.3 steals and 5.1 blocks per game. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/Ark_Season_2025-26.pdf))

From a traditional scouting lens, Arkansas is a Calipari pace-and-pressure offense built around one elite lead guard, downhill wings, and constant paint pressure. The measurable tendencies are specific: Arkansas scores 89.9 per game, has 17.0 assists per game, and gets to the line 794 times in 34 games, a major volume indicator for a dribble-drive attack. In the January 3 win over Tennessee, Arkansas won despite just 38.5% second-half shooting because it generated 25-of-27 free throws; Darius Acuff Jr. scored 19 second-half points and Malique Ewin scored 10 in the half, a strong clue that Calipari leaned into spread ball-screen and straight-line rim attacks instead of settling. In the February 14 win over Auburn, Arkansas scored 52 points in the paint, shot 27-of-40 on two-pointers, and finished with 19 assists against only five turnovers, which points to a heavy menu of middle ball screens, slot drives, and baseline dunker-spot finishes for Billy Richmond III, Ewin, and Trevon Brazile. In the March 4 win over Texas, Arkansas opened on a 19-4 run and piled up a season-high 38 fastbreak points plus 21 assists; that is the clearest named example of the Razorbacks at their best in early offense, turning stops into hit-ahead attacks and rim runs before the defense gets set. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/Ark_Season_2025-26.pdf))

Personnel defines the scheme. Acuff is the engine at 22.9 points and 216 assists, with 85 made threes at 44.5%; he is both primary creator and late-clock shot maker. Meleek Thomas gives Arkansas a second perimeter scorer at 15.4 points and 42.1% from three. Brazile spaces as a pick-and-pop forward while still giving vertical play at the rim; he averages 13.2 points, 7.4 rebounds, and 53 blocks. Richmond is the slash-and-finish wing at 11.0 points on 55.6% shooting, and Ewin is the interior changeup at 9.6 points on 59.1% shooting with 182 rebounds in only 20.0 minutes per game. The structure is simple but specific: Acuff initiates, Thomas spaces, Brazile and Ewin screen or dive, and Richmond cuts behind help. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/Ark_Season_2025-26.pdf))

Defensively, Arkansas plays to length, rim protection, and turnover avoidance rather than pure gambling. The statistical markers are clear: opponents shoot only .317 from three, Arkansas averages 5.1 blocks and 7.3 steals, and the Hogs force 11.5 turnovers per game while committing just 9.0 themselves. The Tennessee game showed the frontcourt shape of the defense: Ewin had five blocked shots, including four in the second half, and Arkansas survived a game where Tennessee actually produced 24 fastbreak points. The Auburn win is another documented example of defensive adjustment inside the game: after Auburn’s Tahaad Pettiford and KeShawn Murphy hurt them early, Arkansas opened the second half on a 15-2 burst and limited Murphy to just four second-half points while adding eight blocked shots in the half. That suggests Calipari’s group is most effective when the back line is set and Brazile/Ewin can erase mistakes at the rim. The weakness is physical frontcourts: Florida beat Arkansas 56-44 in paint points and 51-31 on the glass on February 28. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/Ark_Season_2025-26.pdf))

Calipari’s coaching philosophy is visible in documented game-to-game and halftime adjustments. Against Tennessee on January 3, Arkansas trailed 7-0 immediately, then answered with a 9-0 run; later, during an 11-0 second-half run, Karter Knox, Ewin, and Acuff all scored inside the flow while the Razorbacks defended without fouling. Against Auburn on February 14, the adjustment was even sharper: after losing 95-73 at Auburn on January 10, Arkansas won the rematch 88-75 by flipping the shot profile, dominating two-point efficiency and posting 10 assists with zero turnovers in the second half. After the double-overtime loss at Alabama on February 18, Arkansas responded three days later by beating Missouri 94-86; Richmond scored 21, Acuff 20, and when Missouri cut it to 78-73 with 6:28 left, Arkansas answered with a 6-0 sequence from Acuff, Brazile, and Ewin to regain control. That bounce-back is a concrete example of Calipari restoring order after a high-possession loss. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/18-hogs-take-down-19-20-tennessee-in-sec-opener/))

Clutch execution is a real strength because Arkansas has a true closer. The best example is February 18 at Alabama: Arkansas lost 117-115 in double overtime, but Acuff forced overtime by hitting his sixth three to tie the game at 95-95, then kept answering in the second overtime of a game that was tied five times in that period. Even in defeat, that game showed Arkansas can function in elite-possession games because it has a guard who can create his own shot late. The Tennessee win on January 3 is another strong late-game sample: despite a one-point halftime edge and multiple lead changes in both halves, Arkansas separated late with that 11-0 run and shot 25-of-27 at the line. The Auburn rematch also qualifies; after Auburn cut the margin to 63-55 and then 65-57, Arkansas did not unravel and closed the game from there. Missouri on February 21 is another practical tournament indicator: Missouri got within five at 78-73, but Arkansas answered immediately and built the lead to 14 with 2:02 left. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/acuff-jr-scores-49-in-double-ot-loss-at-25-bama/))

Key players, with recent form and standout moments: Acuff is the headline player and one of the country’s most dangerous freshman guards. He averages 22.9 points and 6.4 assists per game, and his recent ceiling games are elite: 49 points at Alabama on February 18, then 28 points and 13 assists versus Texas on March 4, making him, per Arkansas, the only high-major player this season with a 28-point, 13-assist game. He also had 31 points and seven assists in the Auburn win. Richmond is the tournament X-factor; he scored a career-high 25 against Auburn on 12-of-15 shooting with five dunks and three steals, then had 21 against Missouri and entered the Florida game on a five-game streak of 20-plus points. Brazile remains the two-way matchup problem; he had a career-high 28 against Texas on 9-of-11 shooting with three made threes, seven rebounds, and three blocks. Ewin is the interior stabilizer, shown best by 12 points, six rebounds, and five blocks against Tennessee. Thomas is the secondary shot-maker; he averages 15.4 and scored 18 against Tennessee, with 12 in the first half when Arkansas needed half-court scoring. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/Ark_Season_2025-26.pdf))

Notable wins: Tennessee on January 3 was revealing because Arkansas beat a ranked opponent 86-75 even while allowing 24 fastbreak points; that showed composure and free-throw reliability. Auburn on February 14 was more revealing tactically because Arkansas corrected a 22-point road loss from the first meeting and won by 13 behind 52 paint points and a clean 19-to-5 assist-turnover line. Texas on March 4 showed Arkansas’s offensive ceiling: 105 points, a 19-4 start, 38 fastbreak points, and a 28-and-13 masterpiece from Acuff. Missouri on February 21 showed rebound ability after adversity, arriving just after the Alabama heartbreak and producing a controlled 94-86 win. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/18-hogs-take-down-19-20-tennessee-in-sec-opener/))

Notable losses: the 95-73 loss at Auburn on January 10 exposed Arkansas when opponents win the athleticism battle and turn them over into transition. The 117-115 double-overtime loss at Alabama on February 18 showed a different issue: even a historic Acuff game could not overcome defensive slippage in a track meet. The February 28 loss at Florida showed the most tournament-relevant weakness against elite size and depth, with Arkansas losing the rebounding battle 51-31 and giving up 56 paint points. Those three games together say Arkansas is dangerous in open-floor games but can be worn down by physical, deep front lines if the whistles or boards go the wrong way. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/AUB-Game-25-Arkansas-Notes.pdf?utm_source=openai))

As for John Calipari’s NCAA Tournament history, Arkansas’s official bio states he has taken 24 teams to the NCAA Tournament, with 16 Sweet 16 appearances, 12 Elite Eights, six Final Fours, three national title game appearances, and one national championship. The same official bio notes that by reaching the Sweet 16 in his first Arkansas season in 2025, he improved to 59 NCAA Tournament wins. In year two at Arkansas, that history matters because this roster plays like a Calipari March team: a star lead guard, NBA-caliber wings, shot blocking, and enough late-game creation to survive close possessions. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/coache/john-calipari/))

Bottom line: Arkansas is not just talented; it is specifically hard to prepare for because Acuff can beat switches, traps, and drop coverage, while Brazile and Ewin give Calipari two different screen partners and Richmond has become a reliable downhill finisher. If the Razorbacks control the glass and keep the game in their preferred pace band, they have the shot creation and rim protection profile of a second-weekend team. If an opponent can maul them on the boards the way Florida did, the ceiling drops. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/Ark_Season_2025-26.pdf))

Arkansas enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a legitimately strong but slightly profile-splitting team: high enough in the predictive systems to project as a dangerous second-weekend caliber opponent, yet not quite as dominant statistically as the brand name, SEC pedigree, and raw talent might imply. Across the major résumé and predictive dashboards that are publicly accessible, the Razorbacks rate as a clear top-20 team nationally. Warren Nolan’s 2026 team sheet lists Arkansas at NET No. 18, with predictive marks of KenPom No. 17, BPI No. 21, and Bart Torvik T-Rank No. 20. That same team sheet shows a Division I record of 19-6 at the time of that snapshot, with a NET strength of schedule rank of 16 and non-conference SOS rank of 27. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Arkansas&utm_source=openai))

By Selection Sunday-era results, the broader Warren Nolan team page reflects an even fuller résumé: Arkansas finished 26-8 overall, 13-5 in the SEC, 17-1 at home, 5-5 on the road, and 4-2 on neutral floors. The Razorbacks were 8-2 in their last 10 games entering the tournament, on a five-game winning streak, with overall SOS ranked No. 9 and non-conference SOS No. 6 by Warren Nolan’s RPI-based schedule metric. That page lists Arkansas at NET No. 15, ELO No. 9, and RPI No. 7, plus quadrant records of 8-8 in Q1, 8-0 in Q2, 4-0 in Q3, and 6-0 in Q4. In other words, the Hogs paired very good top-end competitiveness with almost no bad losses whatsoever. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-clubhouse?team=Arkansas))

The cleanest macro interpretation is that Arkansas has the résumé of a protected-seed type team and the predictive profile of a team sitting roughly in the national 15-25 band. That gap matters. Conventional wisdom may see Arkansas as a classic SEC bruiser with overwhelming two-way efficiency, but the accessible numerical profile is a little more modest: strong, balanced, and difficult to beat, though not necessarily elite in every possession-based category. Warren Nolan’s advanced net rating page places Arkansas at +14.3, 31st nationally. That is good enough to support tournament advancement, but it is not the profile of a top-five juggernaut. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-net-rating?utm_source=openai))

On the possession-level offensive style markers that are available, Arkansas looks more pressure-and-glass oriented than spacing-heavy. Warren Nolan’s 2026 three-point attempt rate page lists Arkansas at 0.352, indicating that only 35.2% of its field-goal attempts come from three. That is a relatively moderate-to-low perimeter volume in the modern game and suggests an offense that does not rely on bombing away from deep. At the same time, Arkansas posts a 32.2% offensive rebound rate, a very strong figure that places it among the better offensive rebounding teams in the country. Its total rebound rate is 51.3%, solid but not overwhelming overall, which implies the real edge is on the offensive glass more than in complete board control. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-3pa-rate?utm_source=openai))

The shooting efficiency data that can be directly accessed reinforces that picture. Arkansas owns a 52.2% effective field-goal rate on Warren Nolan’s advanced eFG% leaderboard. That is good, but not elite; it reads more like a well-rounded offense than an unstoppable one. Put together with the lower three-point attempt rate, the likely offensive identity is this: Arkansas creates value through rim pressure, second shots, physicality, and enough shotmaking to stay efficient, rather than through extreme shot-selection math. That can be a very tournament-friendly formula when whistles are consistent and offensive rebounding carries over, but it can also create volatility against elite half-court defenses that take away the paint and finish possessions. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2025/stats-adv-efg-percent?utm_source=openai))

Exact public values for adjusted offensive efficiency, adjusted defensive efficiency, pace, turnover percentage, and free-throw rate were not broadly exposed in the searchable results I could access, but the available rankings still let us infer a fair amount. Arkansas’ predictive placements — KenPom 17, BPI 21, Torvik 20 — strongly suggest a team that is above average on both ends rather than carried exclusively by either offense or defense. Its +14.3 net rating rank of 31st supports the idea of a balanced good team rather than an elite specialized one. And because the résumé metrics are slightly stronger than the predictive ones, Arkansas appears to have outperformed its raw possession dominance somewhat, likely by winning close high-leverage games and avoiding résumé-damaging losses. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Arkansas&utm_source=openai))

Recent form is one of the biggest positives in the file. Arkansas closed 8-2 over its last 10 and built a five-game winning streak into the bracket. That is meaningful because the last-10 record aligns with a team whose underlying quality may have been stabilizing late, rather than fading. Even without a fully accessible last-10 adjusted efficiency split, the win-loss trend indicates Arkansas was moving in the right direction entering March. For a tournament forecast, that matters almost as much as full-season average efficiency, especially for a roster whose eye-test appeal often comes from physicality and matchup pressure. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-clubhouse?team=Arkansas))

The biggest divergence from conventional wisdom is probably this: Arkansas looks less like a high-octane shot-making machine and more like a rugged, résumé-rich, possession-winning team. The public numbers suggest they are not built on overwhelming three-point volume or outlier shooting efficiency. Instead, the profile is built on schedule toughness, consistent winning across quadrant tiers, strong offensive rebounding, and enough overall quality to land in the top 15-20 of the national ranking ecosystem. That can make Arkansas seem more dangerous in bracket play than some cleaner-looking efficiency teams, because physical offensive rebounding and a battle-tested schedule often translate well to single-elimination settings. But it also means the Razorbacks may be somewhat more vulnerable than public perception against opponents that protect the defensive glass and force them into jump-shot offense. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Arkansas&utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: Arkansas’ 2026 tournament statistical profile is that of a strong, tested SEC team with top-20 consensus ranking strength, top-10 caliber résumé indicators in some systems, a top-10-to-top-16 strength of schedule depending on metric, a 52.2% eFG%, a 32.2% offensive rebound rate, and a comparatively modest 35.2% three-point attempt rate. The Razorbacks’ recent 8-2 surge and excellent quadrant distribution make them more dangerous than a simple net-rating rank might imply. If you are building a forecasting model, Arkansas should grade as a team with real Sweet 16 viability and upset equity against more aesthetically efficient opponents, while still carrying some offensive ceiling questions if second-chance points and interior pressure are neutralized. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-clubhouse?team=Arkansas))
matchup-analyst:
Arkansas enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 26-8 and looks exactly like a John Calipari tournament offense built around an elite lead guard: high-efficiency creation, low turnover volume, and constant pressure on the rim before the defense gets set. The raw season profile is strong: 89.9 points per game, .500 FG, .389 from three, 17.0 assists per game, only 9.0 turnovers per game, and a 1.9 assist/turnover ratio. They also average 19.25 fast-break points per game, which Arkansas’ own game notes list as third-best nationally at that point in the season, while allowing just 10.25 fast-break points per game. The engine is Darius Acuff Jr. at 22.9 points and 6.5 assists per game on .486/.445/.804 shooting, with secondary scoring from Meleek Thomas (15.4 ppg, .421 from three) and frontcourt finishing/rim pressure from Trevon Brazile (13.2 ppg, 7.4 rpg, 53 blocks) and Malique Ewin (.591 FG). ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/teamcume.htm))

Style of play: Arkansas wants the game fast, spaced, and guard-driven. The numbers show a team that does not waste possessions: 1091 made field goals against only 306 turnovers for the season, plus 578 assists. Acuff alone has 216 assists; Meleek Thomas adds 84; D.J. Wagner adds 76. That means the offense is not random chaos — it is pace with organization. They are most dangerous when Acuff collapses the first line, Brazile or Ewin finishes inside, and kick-outs find Thomas or Acuff. Their best offensive examples are 108 against South Carolina, 105 against Texas, 99 against Texas A&M, 94 against Missouri, and 115 in the double-overtime loss at Alabama. In SEC play through mid-January, Arkansas was already second in conference field-goal percentage at .496, and by late February Arkansas game notes listed the Razorbacks first in the SEC in overall FG% and 2PT%. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/teamcume.htm))

The specific tactics that disrupt Arkansas are: 1) win the glass decisively, 2) make Acuff finish over length instead of spraying passes, and 3) force them to play against a set half-court defense for long stretches. The evidence is concrete. Auburn beat Arkansas 95-73 while outrebounding them 37-28, winning paint points 48-28 and second-chance points 18-9. Florida blasted Arkansas 111-77 while winning the rebounding battle 51-31. Kentucky’s postgame notes from the January 31 game say UK won the glass 35-26 and forced an early Arkansas timeout after racing to a 14-5 lead. When Arkansas loses physically on the backboard, its skill edge shrinks fast. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/AUB-Game-25-Arkansas-Notes.pdf))

Press vulnerability: there is not strong public evidence that Arkansas is broadly vulnerable to pressure in the usual sense of coughing the ball up. In fact, the opposite is better-supported. Arkansas averages only 9.0 turnovers per game, and the staff highlighted single-digit turnover games against LSU (8), Oklahoma (6), Kentucky (4), Mississippi State (7), Vanderbilt (7), and South Carolina (4). That suggests a full-court press is not your primary winning lever unless you have unusual size at the point of attack and can trap Acuff late-clock rather than early-possession. Arkansas’ own notes say they are 13-1 when keeping turnovers to single digits. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/teamcume.htm))

Zone vulnerability: again, there is limited public play-type data available in official sources, so the safest inference is from their shot profile and game-by-game 3-point outcomes. Arkansas is generally equipped to punish soft zone because Acuff shoots .445 from three, Meleek Thomas .421, and Karter Knox .377, while the team shoots .389 from deep overall. But there are clear examples where compact half-court defenses dragged them into lower-percentage jump shooting: at Georgia Arkansas went 5-of-21 from three, at Oklahoma 2-of-17, and versus Kentucky 3-of-14, all cited in Arkansas game notes. Those are not proof of “zone” by themselves, but they are proof that Arkansas becomes more ordinary when opponents wall off the lane and make them live on settled perimeter volume instead of paint touches and drive-kick rhythm. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/teamcume.htm))

Preferred pace: Arkansas prefers a high-possession game. The schedule itself shows this in scoring environment: 109 vs Southern, 115 vs Jackson State, 108 vs South Carolina, 99 vs Texas A&M, 105 vs Texas, 115 in 2OT at Alabama. Their fast-break scoring supports that preference. To force the opposite, opponents need to shorten the game with offensive rebounding, half-court shot quality, and transition floor balance. Michigan State’s 69-66 win and Duke’s 80-71 win are examples of opponents keeping Arkansas below its season average by 23.9 and 18.9 points respectively. Auburn’s 95-73 win is different: that game was not slow, but Auburn forced Arkansas to play reactively and physically rather than on its own terms. So the best anti-Arkansas formula is not merely “slow it down,” but “make every Arkansas possession start against five defenders.” ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/teamcume.htm))

Position-by-position size and athleticism: at point guard, Acuff (33 starts, 35.2 mpg) is the skill mismatch because of 22.9 ppg and 6.5 apg, but bigger guards can attack him on the other end and body him into harder finishes. At the scoring-wing spots, Meleek Thomas gives Arkansas shot-making and steals (49), while Billy Richmond III gives downhill size and efficiency (.556 FG). At forward, Brazile is the major athletic mismatch: 7.4 rebounds and 53 blocks, plus he can step out and hit .360 from three. Ewin is the interior efficiency piece at .591 FG with 182 rebounds. The vulnerability is that Arkansas’ true center rotation is not overwhelming in bulk rebounding; Nick Pringle averages only 3.9 rebounds in 19.0 minutes, and Ewin is undersized compared with the elite national glass-eaters Arkansas has struggled with. Florida’s Rueben Chinyelu grabbing 16 rebounds in the 111-77 game is the clearest example. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/teamcume.htm))

Isolation vs. team offense tendencies: official public sources do not provide a full Synergy play-type table here, so I cannot honestly assign exact isolation-possession percentage without inventing it. What the verified data does show is that Arkansas leans more team offense than pure iso: 578 assists on 1091 made field goals means 53.0% of Arkansas makes were assisted, and the team assist/turnover ratio is 1.9. Acuff’s 216 assists and Arkansas’ 17.0 assists per game indicate a drive-and-create offense, not a stagnant one-man attack. That said, late-clock and close-game usage clearly consolidates around Acuff, as seen by his 49-point explosion at Alabama and 37 against Oklahoma in the SEC Tournament. So the offense is primarily organized team creation until it becomes Acuff isolation/ball-screen bailout in leverage moments. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/teamcume.htm))

Transition offense and defense frequency: Arkansas’ official notes give the best available public measure — 19.25 fast-break points per game on offense and only 10.25 allowed on defense. They also logged 30+ fast-break points five times, including 32 vs South Carolina, 32 vs Southern, 30 vs Central Arkansas, 34 vs Jackson State, and 31 vs James Madison. That confirms transition is not occasional; it is a core source of margin. But Auburn showed Arkansas can be beaten in its preferred environment too, with Auburn winning fast-break points 15-13 while also dominating paint and second-chance scoring. Florida’s blowout is another warning sign: once Arkansas stopped controlling the efficiency battle, their own pace preference turned into a liability. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/GM-25-vs-Auburn.pdf))

Coaching adaptability: there is evidence Calipari’s staff can adjust within tournament settings, though “mid-series” is not literally applicable in single-elimination NCAA play. Arkansas closed the season with three straight SEC Tournament wins: 82-79 over Oklahoma, 93-90 over Ole Miss in overtime, and 86-75 over Vanderbilt. That shows short-turnaround game-planning adaptability. More specifically, the team responded to the January 10 Auburn loss with a later 88-75 home win over Auburn on February 14, a strong example of staff adjustment to a previously losing matchup. Arkansas also followed the 111-77 loss at Florida by beating Texas 105-85 four days later. Those are practical examples of recalibration rather than stubbornness. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/stats/mbb/2025-26/teamcume.htm))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Arkansas, you must do four things. First, own the defensive glass and punish them on the offensive glass; Auburn (+9 on the boards) and Florida (+20) are the templates. Second, build your shell around Acuff’s paint touches — show length, shrink gaps, and make him score over bodies instead of creating assisted threes and dunks. Florida held Arkansas to 40% overall and 31% from three, with Acuff at 6-of-19. Third, get back in transition every possession; Arkansas’ fast-break scoring is too large a share of its offensive identity to ignore. Fourth, attack their frontcourt physically with true size. Chinyelu’s 16 rebounds against Arkansas is the clearest model. If you fail on the glass or let Acuff play downhill in early offense, Arkansas can hang 90+ on anyone. If you force them into a half-court, one-shot game and win the rebounding battle decisively, they become beatable.
